extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers, corpus creators, and biomedical annotators working on automated detection/annotation of spin in randomized controlled trial (RCT) publications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and annotation scheme for creating a corpus and automatic/ manual annotation pipeline to detect 'spin' (misleading/incomplete reporting) in biomedical RCT articles, with particular focus on abstracts. Covers annotation targets, annotation granularity, tool requirements, pre-annotation and human validation tasks, and decision rules for marking incoherence/incompleteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading reporting of study results
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three main types of spin: presenting study results in a misleading way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtypes include: selective reporting of outcomes (omission of the primary outcome; focus on statistically significant results different from the main outcome); occulting adverse events; misleading reporting of study design; linguistic spin (beautifying formulations); discarding limitations; selective citation of other studies. Examples and annotation should capture these forms when present in abstracts or results/conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate interpretation of the results
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive forms of spin where conclusions drawn are not supported by statistical evidence or appropriate inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: claiming a beneficial effect despite statistically non-significant results; claiming an equivalent effect for non-significant results; claiming safety for statistically non-significant safety outcomes; concluding benefit despite no comparison test performed; interpreting according to statistical significance instead of clinical relevance. Annotators should flag these interpretive mismatches between reported statistics and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrapolating beyond the population, interventions or outcomes actually assessed in the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes inadequate extrapolation from trial sample/intervention/outcome to a larger or different population/intervention/outcome and making inadequate implications for clinical practice. Such extrapolations should be annotated when conclusions extend beyond evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete reporting (omissions expected in well-reported abstracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of information that is normally expected in a well-reported abstract and that facilitates detection of spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key omissions of interest: absence of a clear definition of the primary outcome; missing results for the primary outcome; missing reporting of non-significant secondary outcomes; lack of explicit information about adverse events (their absence should be stated). Note: omission of other details (design, methods, statistical tests) is considered a 'spin facilitator' rather than spin per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incoherent reporting (discrepancies and inconsistencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistencies between different sources/parts of the article or between design and reporting that indicate possible spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples to detect and annotate: primary outcome in registry differs from primary outcome in text; patient population in abstract does not match studied population (age/gender/etc.); reported results inconsistent with trial design; treatments reported as similar though design is not equivalence/non-inferiority; inappropriate within-group comparisons; focus on significant secondary outcomes instead of the primary; positive conclusions when primary outcome is not significant. Annotations should be established by checking abstract vs body vs registry.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of trial data elements to extract
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured set of data describing a trial that should be extracted/annotated to enable spin assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements include: information about interventions (name, dosage, schedule, duration); participants (age, gender, condition, nationality/ethnicity, recruitment country/region, inclusion/exclusion criteria); trial methods/design (allocation concealment/type, blinding, sample sizes, study type/subtype, phase, statistical tests); trial objectives/outcomes (measurement methods and time points); registration data (number, time); financing/sponsors; hypothesis and hypothesis type; general information/medical domain; summary. Additional categories relevant to spin: limitations and reported statistical measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation algorithm / main annotation steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Pipeline steps for automatic and manual annotation aimed at spin detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main steps: divide article into title/abstract/body and find results and conclusions within the abstract; identify positive evaluation of the studied treatment in results/conclusions; extract trial data relevant to spin (outcomes, patient population, statistical significance); extract relations between trial elements (e.g. outcome linked to its statistical significance); extract specific constructions possibly related to spin (similarity statements, within-group comparisons, recommendations); final assessment: check if information in results/conclusions corresponds to extracted trial data (e.g., are pre-defined outcomes reported correctly, is positive evaluation supported by statistically significant results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation scheme levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-level annotation scheme implemented in XML to capture structure, trial data and spin indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levels include: 1) Document type (article/registry entry). 2) Structural information (journal, title, authors, abstract, body, bibliography; mark Results and Conclusions within abstracts). 3) Elements describing the trial (interventions, outcomes, population, methods). 4) Relations linking elements (e.g., outcome to its measurement/time point or intervention to dosage). 5) Particular constructions (positive evaluations, similarity statements, within-group comparisons). 6) Annotation for spin (relations or empty tags indicating missing expected relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome tagging attributes (Type and Status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific tagging scheme for outcomes to distinguish primary/secondary/undefined and declared vs reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome tag attributes: Type can be Prim (primary), Sec (secondary) or None (undefined). Status can be Declared (explicitly stated as an outcome in text) or Reported (outcome only appears in results/conclusion without being declared). Example tags and usage are provided. Guidance also states that the primary outcome should be presented first regardless of statistical significance when evaluating correct reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation annotation for spin (TimeML-like empty tags with spin attribute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method for encoding whether expected relations between trial elements are present or missing to mark spin/incompleteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empty tags that reference IDs of fragments that are linked when reporting is correct; if incoherence/incompleteness, tag contains ID of present fragment only. These relation tags have an attribute 'spin' set to 'yes' or 'no'. For omissions in abstracts (e.g., missing primary outcome), use empty tags to mark the omitted information type (no ID reference needed). This enables computing a 'spin' attribute at text or fragment level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation granularity: annotate smallest representative fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline on the size of text fragments to annotate for constructions related to spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer annotating the smallest possible fragments (word/phrase level) that are indicators of relevant constructions rather than whole propositions; motivation: simpler and clearer for annotators, and easier to expand to sentence level later. Provide examples showing annotation of single words/phrases indicating constructions (e.g., 'appears to reduce', subject phrases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular constructions of interest to annotate
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific textual constructions that signal spin or are useful for spin assessment and should be annotated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: positive evaluations of treatment (positive language in results/conclusions); statements of similarity between treatments about efficacy or safety; within-group comparisons; comparative constructions reporting trial results (compared patient groups, compared treatments, outcomes used for comparison); descriptions of studied population; recommendations to use treatment. Examples and XML annotation snippets are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-annotation tasks and simplified human annotation questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Set of simpler, independent tasks/questions for human annotators built on automatic pre-annotation to reduce complexity for non-specialist annotators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planned per-item survey/question tasks include: validation/correction of primary outcomes found at pre-annotation; validation/correction of reported outcomes; establishing if two extracted outcomes refer to the same concept; identification of similarity statements in Results and Conclusions; identification of within-group comparisons in Results and Conclusions; identification of other positive evaluations of the studied treatment. Use a web-survey tool (e.g., LimeSurvey) to present pre-annotated fragments with short guidelines per question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator skill stratification and task assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Which annotation tasks can be performed by non-specialists vs which require medical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks suitable for annotators without medical expertise: explicit descriptions of outcomes, mentions of patient population, extraction of statistical measures (p-values), confidence intervals. Tasks likely requiring medical/domain knowledge: reported outcomes (interpretation), similarity statements, within-group comparisons, and evaluations related to treatment. The final spin annotation is most difficult and may require domain experts due to disagreement among experts on definitions of spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation tool selection criteria and usability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for annotation tools and practical considerations for tool choice for this task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionality requirement: tools must be able to capture relations, potentially embedded relations (so tools not allowing relation annotation are inappropriate). Glozz was chosen for its relation/scheme support but has usability/installation/training burdens for non-linguist annotators. Therefore the authors prefer a survey-based approach for simpler tasks to lower the training barrier (LimeSurvey). Tool choice should consider training time and ease of access for medical community annotators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rules: when mismatch is spin vs acceptable change
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines to decide whether discrepancies constitute spin or are acceptable when justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mismatch (e.g., change of outcomes between abstract and article or registry) is not spin if it has valid scientific justification provided in the article; extraction of such justifications is outside current scope. The authors also note disagreement among experts on whether absence of an explicit primary outcome in the abstract is definite spin or merely incomplete reporting; thus the project focuses on annotating components (outcomes, constructions) rather than definitively labeling spin in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example assessment procedure for primary outcome-related spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete stepwise procedure to assess spin related to primary outcomes using the annotation scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps provided: 1) Check and mark if there is a definition of the primary outcome in the abstract (absence -> incomplete reporting). 2) Check and mark if the declared primary outcome is present among reported outcomes (if present -> correct reporting). 3) Check and mark if the primary outcome is presented according to its importance (should be presented first regardless of significance; if presented after significant secondary outcomes -> incoherent reporting/focus on secondary outcomes). The example demonstrates how these steps lead to annotation decisions (incomplete reporting, correct reporting, incoherent reporting).
